entries.name: ball lightning
entries.senseHere: A glowing ball seen during thunderstorms that lasts a few seconds and vanishes, sometimes leaving traces. It has never been explained.
entries.background: Eyewitnesses have reported it for centuries, but almost no photographs or instrument recordings exist. Many theories have been proposed and none is accepted.

entries.name: François Arago
entries.background: French astronomer and physicist who wrote Sur le tonnerre in 1837. He collected early reports of ball lightning and is credited with the term.

entries.name: Walther Brand
entries.background: German school official who wrote Der Kugelblitz (1923), the only German-language monograph on ball lightning. It collected many older reports.

entries.name: Stanley Singer
entries.background: Author of the 1971 book The Nature of Ball Lightning. It collected many case reports.

entries.name: Stenhoff
entries.background: Author of the 1999 book Ball Lightning: An Unsolved Problem in Atmospheric Physics, with about 2400 references.

entries.name: Rakov and Uman
entries.background: Vladimir Rakov and Martin Uman wrote a major lightning handbook in 2003. Its chapter 20 reviews ball lightning, and Uman also led a lightning field experiment at Camp Blanding.

entries.name: Vladimir Lvovich Bychkov
entries.background: Russian physics professor who keeps a database of Russian ball lightning case reports. He also reported his own sighting.

entries.name: Prairie Meteorite Network
entries.background: A US network of cameras that photographed the night sky for meteors. A search of its records found two probable ball lightning events.

entries.name: ALDIS
aliases: Austrian lightning detection and information system
entries.background: Austria's network of sensors that records when and where lightning strikes, and with what current.

entries.name: BLIDS
entries.background: Germany's lightning location service, which detects strikes using a network of sensors.

entries.name: Pyotr Leonidovich Kapitsa
entries.background: Russian Nobel Prize-winning physicist who proposed a theory of ball lightning.

entries.name: Wilhelm von Haidinger
entries.background: Austrian geologist and mineralogist in Vienna. He reported glowing balls seen during a storm in 1868.

entries.name: Axel D. Wittmann
entries.background: German astrophysicist at Göttingen who saw ball lightning as a child in 1951. He reported it to the journal Nature.

entries.name: Othniel Charles Marsh
entries.background: American palaeontologist at Yale and president of the US National Academy of Sciences. He saw a ball of fire on a yacht in 1878.

entries.name: Walther Gerlach
entries.background: German experimental physicist known for the Stern–Gerlach experiment of 1922, which showed that atoms in a magnetic field take only certain discrete spin orientations.

entries.name: Roger Clifton Jennison
entries.background: British radio astronomer and later professor of electronics. He reported a glowing sphere drifting down an airliner aisle in 1963.

entries.name: Georg Wilhelm Richmann
entries.background: Baltic German physicist in St Petersburg who was killed by lightning in 1753 while experimenting with atmospheric electricity.

entries.name: Jean-Martin Charcot
entries.background: French physician and founder of modern neurology at the Salpêtrière Hospital in Paris. He taught Sigmund Freud.

entries.name: keraunoparalysis
entries.senseHere: Short-lived paralysis and other nerve effects after a lightning strike, as opposed to lasting nervous disorders that follow.

entries.name: Dorstone case
entries.background: A 1936 report from Herefordshire, England, of a red-hot ball that fell into a tub of water and made it boil. The water volume allowed researchers to estimate the ball's energy.

entries.name: Poughquag case
entries.background: A 2008 sighting in New York State of a blue ball near a glass porch door. Later tests of the glass estimated the ball's radiation output.

entries.name: Camp Blanding experiment
entries.background: A 2008 experiment at a Florida military base in which rockets trailing wires triggered lightning onto over 100 materials on the ground. It was designed to see whether ball-like effects could be produced.

entries.name: Qinghai spectrum
entries.background: A 2012 recording on China's Qinghai Plateau in which video cameras with spectrometers captured a ball lightning event and its light spectrum.

entries.name: Nikitin Mitino case
entries.background: A 2015 event in a Moscow district in which three people filmed a glowing object with phones. Triangulating the videos gave its height and speed.
